slides.text: When the true moon was shattered during the First Sundering, the guild of Master Horologists forged a replacement from brass, mirrors, and sixty thousand interlocking gears to guide the tides and warm the tundra. For four centuries, the great luminary had rotated on its celestial pendulum, tended by generation after generation of Moonkeepers who walked its bronze catwalks with oil cans and chamois cloths, miles above the sleeping continents.

On the night of the Winter Solstice, the main escapement wheel shuddered and ground to a sudden halt. The tides froze against the coastal harbors; panic spread across the world below as the artificial luminescence began to sputter into blackness. Armed with a brass spanner, young apprentice Ilya descended into the central gear casing, expecting to find a broken tooth or a snapped counterweight. Instead, deep inside the bronze ribcage of the moon, she saw something that took her breath away.

Curled between the massive iron flywheels, asleep atop a bed of discarded copper cogs, was a white celestial moth with wings the span of a galleon. It had nested inside the machinery to escape the solar winds, its velvet antenna tangled delicately in the gear teeth. Ilya looked down at her wrench, then gently reached out with her bare hand to disentangle the soft wing. As the moth stirred and breathed, the entire moon began to hum with living light.
